I call to order the informal meeting of the working group on strengthening and revitalization of the work of the General Assembly. We warmly welcome you and our speakers here today. This meeting is held in accordance with General Assembly resolution 79/327 of 5 September 2025, which called to continue the practice of the convening of an annual interactive dialogue between Member States and the Secretariat. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, good morning. It is my pleasure in my capacity as co-chair of the working group on the strengthening and revitalization of the work of the General Assembly to welcome you to this year's annual interactive dialogue between member states and the secretariat. This dialogue provides a valuable opportunity for an open and practical exchange on the respective and complementary roles of Member States and the Secretariat in supporting the effective functioning of the General Assembly. As we begin this session, we are pleased to have with us colleagues from DGACM, DGCC, DSS, DOS and DMSPC. We thank you for your continued support and look forward to hearing your perspectives. Today's discussion will focus in particular on the implementation of resolution 79/327, the impact of the liquidity crisis, initiatives to strengthen support to the General Assembly, and other challenges affecting the efficiency and effectiveness of our work. We hope this will be a candid and constructive dialogue with particular focus on practical solutions and opportunities for improvement. I encourage delegations to keep their interventions brief and focused, allowing ample time for an interactive exchange with our secretariat colleagues. With that, I am pleased to open the dialogue and look forward to a productive discussion. Thank you. I now give the floor to my colleague, my co-chair, Ambassador Furuta.

Well, thank you very much, dear colleagues. Not much to add. We will go straight to business. And indeed, this meeting as well is part of the implementation efforts of member states of resolution 79327. And I think it would be also a good time for us to reflect on on best practices implementing important features and decisions in that resolution. But of course, I'll be looking myself as well forward to the conversation and to the briefing from the senior leadership of the Secretariat on issues that are always of interest to member states. So back to you.
Thank you. At this point, I now give the floor to Ms. Catherine Pollack, Under Secretary General for Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance.

Thank you, Madam Chair, distinguished co-chairs, excellencies, distinguished delegates and colleagues. Good morning. I would like to thank the co-chairs for convening this meeting and for inviting the Department of Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance to brief you. These interactive dialogues are valuable opportunities to ensure that the services and substantive support provided by the Secretariat remains closely aligned with the needs and priorities of Member States, while at the same time enhancing our effectiveness, transparency and responsiveness. As you know, the MSPC does not have a broad mandate to provide direct secretariat support to the General Assembly, except the substantive and technical support that we provide to the Fifth Committee. More broadly, We support the General Assembly in exercising its governance responsibilities by strengthening transparency, accountability, internal controls, and by improving access to timely information on the management of the organization. Over recent years, we have substantially expanded the information and data available to Member States. The UN Secretariat Workforce Portal provides daily updated information on the composition of the Secretariat workforce, including by entity, level and nationality. Information on representation under the system of desirable ranges is also updated monthly. The Budget Information Pilot and Programme Budget Results Dashboard at results.un.org similarly provides Member States with improved access to resource and programmatic performance information. The integrated performance management and reporting capability is also intended to provide greater visibility into program performance as its coverage and adoption are expanded. Through a dedicated UMOJA portal, Member States can also access information on financial contributions. These initiatives reflect the broader direction of our management reforms, simplifying policies and processes, strengthening internal controls, and increasing transparency over the use of resources. Our aim is to give Member States better information with which to perform their governance and decision-making roles. In implementing the relevant provisions of resolution 79/327, we continue to support the General Assembly's objectives relating to equitable geographic distribution and gender parity, and I am pleased to report tangible progress. The number of underrepresented Member States under the system of desirable ranges declined from 36 in 2021 to 31 in December 2024 and to 24 by June 2026. External recruitment from underrepresented Member States increased by approximately one third between 2024 and 2025. And in 2025, for the first time, nationals of underrepresented member states accounted for more than half of all geographical external recruitments. Nevertheless, 21 member states remain unrepresented and sustained attention is therefore necessary. We continue to pursue targeted outreach, talent pipeline and capacity development initiatives, including through purposeful partnership agreements, alongside strengthened workforce planning and greater use of recruitment data. We have also made progress towards gender parity. As of June 2026, women represented 47.5% of internationally recruited staff, bringing the Secretariat within the gender parity range. Women accounted for 52.1% of external recruitments of international staff in 2025. Parity has been achieved at the Under-Secretary-General, Director D2 level and Professional P5 levels. while women's representation at the assistant secretary level increased from 38.6% in 2024 to 44.6% in 2025. Progress is still needed, particularly in peacekeeping operations and traditionally male-dominated occupational areas, including security, technology, logistics, and supply chain functions. These achievements and ambitions must, however, be placed in the context of the continuing liquidity crisis and its impact on mandate delivery. DMSBC has implemented cash conservation measures across our operations. Vacancies have remained unfilled, capacity building activities have had to be reduced, deferred or replaced by virtual delivery. and activities requiring investment in information technology and new digital tools have been slowed or phased over longer periods. This has affected the pace at which we can advance some of the initiatives that I have earlier described, including those relating to geographical representation, gender parity, management reforms and strengthened internal controls. At the same time, DMSBC has an organization-wide responsibility in helping to manage the liquidity situation itself. This requires significant and sustained engagement with entities across the Secretariat on liquidity management, continuous monitoring of expenditure levels, vacancy management, contingency planning, and monitoring mandate implementation. We are therefore affected in two ways: our own capacity is constrained by the liquidity situation, while considerable DMSBC capacity must simultaneously be dedicated to helping the organization manage the same crisis. Simply put, without these constraints, we could do more and move faster. Despite these constraints, we've continued to identify practical ways of improving our direct support to the work of the General Assembly. The Fifth Committee Secretariat has significantly enhanced access to information through improvements to its website and resources available through the e-delegate portal, including the development of a new Fifth Committee info hub. A documentation dashboard now provides links to issued reports and updated information on the status of documentation, including those in the process of translation or awaiting submission. For the upcoming main part of the 81st session, the system covers 164 reports that Member States can filter by session, agenda item and originating department. We've also made the substantial volume of supplementary information easier to access. During the ATS session, supplementary information comprised 26,039 pages covering 2,373 questions. This material is now being consolidated by agenda item so delegations can more readily download and search the information that they require. The Secretariat has also consolidated the Committee's reporting on recommendations adopted at its closing meetings. For the main part of the 80th session, what would previously have required 15 separate reports was presented in a single report. A new outcomes dashboard covering the Committee's work since the 76th session is also planned to be available shortly. These technical improvements have a practical objective, making it easier for delegates to find, understand, and use the information required for their deliberations and decisions. Another important and relatively new area of support concerns programme budget implications, or PBIs. Under the approach adopted by the General Assembly, the Secretariat is increasingly required to provide information on the potential financial implications arising from draft resolutions and decisions during different stages of the negotiating process rather than principally at their conclusion. Earlier visibility of potential resource implications can support more informed negotiations and decision-making by Member States. At the same time, this creates a significant new operational requirement for the Secretariat. It requires financial and program expertise to be available at multiple points during negotiations, sometimes at short notice and across several processes simultaneously. We are working to respond to this request from the General Assembly. We've also continued to strengthen accountability and internal control systems. including in response to requests from the General Assembly. The annual closure rate for Board of Auditors recommendations increased to 73% in 2025, compared with 54% in 2024 and 48% in 2023. This reflects sustained efforts to address oversight recommendations and strengthen management accountability across the Secretariat. In line with General Assembly resolution 79257, the Secretariat is also reviewing the accountability of the first and second lines of defense in human resources and asset management. This work is important in providing member states with assurance that delegated authority is being exercised responsibly, risks are being appropriately identified and managed, and internal controls across the organization remain effective. While progress has been made, liquidity and capacity constraints have affected the pace at which we can take forward some of these improvements. We are exploring technology solutions and new tools to improve efficiency. However, the development and deployment of technological solutions may take longer due to resource constraints. Excellencies, we will continue to look for ways to simplify our processes, make better use of technology and data, and provide Member States with timely and accessible information. But there is an important connection between liquidity, institutional capacity, and effective governance. When vacancies cannot be filled, when investments in technology must be deferred, when capacity building is reduced, and when significant staff resources must be redirected towards managing cash constraints, the pace of improvement inevitably slows. Our responsibility is therefore both to manage these constraints as effectively as possible and to be transparent with Member States about their consequences. We remain committed to doing everything within our capacity to support the General Assembly and Member States. And I look forward to hearing your perspectives and discussion today. Thank you, Madam Co-Chair.
I thank the Under-Secretary-General for Management, Strategy, Policy and Compliance. I now give the floor to Mr. Ian Phillips, Director of News and Media of the Department of Global Communications.

Thank you very much, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Thank you for the opportunity to brief you on our efforts to support the revitalization of the General Assembly and for what I'm sure will be a constructive, interactive dialogue between this ad hoc working group and the Secretariat. We meet at a time of great challenges for the international community against a backdrop of multi-layered intersecting crises. Widespread conflicts, the climate emergency and runaway technology. Challenges only made more difficult to address during a period marked by a questioning of multilateralism. In these strained times, the work of the General Assembly, humanity's one-of-a-kind meeting ground, matters more than ever. Yet in these strained times, it is still hard for this body to make itself heard, to explain its decisions, its resolutions, and recommendations, and to build trust and understanding of our organization with audiences around the world. Raising the visibility of the GA and its work lies at the core of our role at the Department of Global Communications. Yet that task is more difficult than ever. We communicate at a time when contested narratives spread like wildfire, when new cycles move at lightning speeds. and when audiences are bombarded, overwhelmed, and unsure about what to believe. Attention spans are short, community is divided, emotions are running high. It is into this fractured adversarial landscape that we must communicate, and we do so on behalf of this body and for the whole of the United Nations. This is compounded by the organization's ongoing liquidity crisis, which has strained resources and capacity across the department. That said, despite the gaps caused by the budget cuts and hiring freeze, our teams do remain focused on delivering the results the General Assembly expects of us. Against this backdrop, I want to outline three main ways we draw attention to the work of the GA. First, we show it. Second, we record it. Third, we connect it. Let's start with how we show it. We feature and highlight the GA's work across our platforms in the six official languages, whether that is via our UN news output, meetings coverage on the official YouTube channel or on UN.org, the organization's main website. Our UN Web TV team and UN TV team offers live and on-demand streaming of GA open meetings. Meetings coverage offers continuous multilingual reporting, interviews and explainers. Our UNTV and UNIFID facilities provide complete live and packaged broadcast quality coverage to international broadcasters and news agencies, while our UN video explainers and features give viewers direct insights into the work of the GA. This provides content for UN high-level official social media platforms, including the President of the General Assembly. Further, we are responsible for the GA's web presence. Our web services section manages the dedicated multilingual GA website, including pages covering the revitalization process in six languages. With up to six million views a year, our GA pages are some of the most visited parts of UN.org. Meanwhile, our dedicated multilingual general debate site, gadebate.un.org, offers a real-time who is speaking now or next feature plus a full statement archive across sessions. These activities offer the world a ringside seat for the work of the General Assembly, building trust with transparency and comprehension with clarity. Second, let's look at how we record the GA's work. The Dag Hammarskjold Library, the UN Library, provides a complete overview of the UN's work. Updated daily, this database holds more than one million records, including every GA decision, speech, and voting record since 1946. The Library also tracks and organizes a record of the work of each main committee, with every agenda item and voting record saved and easily accessible for posterity. This facility serves as the General Assembly's institutional memory. distributing the digital handbook on past GA practices, preserving records from the office of the President of the General Assembly, and hosting the PGA's morning dialogue sessions. This resource is well loved. Last year, its documents were downloaded more than 65 million times. What's more, the library is already providing one of the key requests put forward by this ad hoc committee. AHWG resolution A/RES/79/327 calls for common reference data for the consolidation of the Assembly. This process involves standardizing names, agenda items, and other documents to facilitate the sharing of information. It's important to note that the UN Library already manages this work. Updated daily, a master list of standardized terms is available at metadata.un.org in six languages. This list feeds automatically into the UN digital library and official document system. To reiterate, this system is already built and functioning. We don't need to reinvent the wheel. Lastly, we connect the work of the GA to audiences around the world. We do that via the media and via our own direct channels. Our media accreditation and liaison unit accredits, escorts and informs thousands of media outlets as they visit us here in New York. And this work reaches its peak, of course, during the high-level week. Last year, MALU approved approximately 3,300 UNGA media pass applications and supported 2,500 members of the media on campus. We also work directly to get the word out to our audiences. We are present in many Member States via our network of UN Information Centres, or UNICs. Well-versed in local languages and context, these teams help relate the work of the General Assembly to audiences on the ground. Whether it's media outreach, tours or educational activities, the UNICs offer vital points of contact to the UN for many people around the world. To note, the liquidity crisis has also led to a decrease in language capacity in some non-official languages, both here at headquarters and at a number of UNICs. However, our teams are working to leverage technology to help fill this gap. Finally, we raise the voice of the GA through our dedicated social media channels. Speaking to more than 70 million followers, we bring the GA into the feeds of audiences around the world. Last year's general debate coverage, for example, alone drew roughly 1,000 posts, more than 1 million engagements, and around 8 million video views. Distinguished delegates, I am looking forward to a constructive discussion in a moment, but I'd like to close by reiterating GGC's commitment to the work of this ad hoc committee. We are dedicated to meeting the challenges of today's communication landscape head on. supporting a GA whose work is seen, understood, and trusted worldwide. Especially at times like these, it is vital we work to ensure the GA's voice echoes far beyond the General Assembly Hall and that our United Nations truly serves the public it represents. Thank you.

I thank the Director of News and Media of the Department of Global Communications. And I now give the floor to Mr. Alessandro Susini, Acting Director of the Division of Administration of the Department for Operational Support.

Excellencies, Co-Chairs, distinguished delegates, colleagues, I am pleased to brief you today on recent and ongoing work undertaken by the Department of Operational Support on behalf of the Under-Secretary-General, Mr. Atul Khare, as unfortunately he could not attend today's meeting due to other commitments. With that said, let me begin by emphasizing our continued commitment to accessibility at the United Nations headquarters. Since 2018, DOS has implemented a complex wide accessibility enhancement program informed by an accessibility survey that identified improvements beyond the capital master plan. Key improvements completed by 2024 included the GA rostrum lift, sidewalk curb cuts, automatic openers at entrance doors to all conference rooms in the conference and general assembly buildings first basement level, double automatic exit gate at the perimeter fence of the building site, and other related improvements. In continuation of these efforts, DOS has recently completed a follow-up assessment report with the on-call architectural firm to identify further improvements that can be realized and implemented going forward. Phase one of the assessment was conducted and finalized in March 2025, identifying accessibility gaps in priority areas, recommending further improvements for the Member States delegates, visitors and staff with disabilities. In addition, in 2025, automatic door openers were installed at the entrances to 10 office floors of the Secretariat building and braille signage was introduced for conference rooms located on staff office floors. Thus, in coordination with relevant departments, secured approval for a five-year accessibility budget. Accessibility features have also been incorporated into the DC2 renovation, phase one of which has already been completed, encompassing four floors with automatic door openers installed at each floor entrance, accessible workspaces, height adjustable desks, accessible meeting rooms and offices, accessible focus booth, and visual and audible emergency notification systems. Turning to the General Assembly Hall, in the context of the sustainable sustainability efforts of being driven by the host country, the existing halogen and metallic metal halide lighting in the GA Hall have become more challenging to replace. In view of this, we have developed a plan to introduce durable energy efficient LED fixtures as a replacement. DOS is continuing a multi-year modernization of the General Assembly Hall and other conference rooms to replace aging infrastructure and upgrade critical conferencing, audiovisual interpretation and broadcast systems. For 2027, DOS has requested approximately $8.1 million to advance those refurbishment efforts, with priority given to the General Assembly Hall due to the importance of as the organizational principal deliberative chamber and conference room seven. The project also includes replacing seating and other furnishings while preserving the whole historic character. DOS also cooperated with the Office of the President of the General Assembly to seek Member States contributions for the refurbishment of the GA Hall. On space and facilities, following the signing of a new lease for the UNDC II building, a complex renovation is being undertaken to ensure the building is made a fit for purpose for the duration of the new lease. In this regard, we are pleased to inform that through the efficiencies created during the renovation, combined with using space available in the United Nations headquarters complex, it is planned to vacate both the Albano and FF buildings when their current leases expire in September and December 2027, respectively. With respect to catering under the new contract, effective 1 January 2026, and consistent with the previous arrangement, catering operations continue to be managed under the management fee model. The new contract, however, includes a provision requiring a transition to a profit and loss model once revenues exceed a specified threshold. Under the profit and loss model, the contractor assumes full responsibility for the financial performance of the operation and receive no financial support from the United Nations in the form of a subsidy. Any operating losses are borne entirely by the contractor without compensation from the United Nations. Conversely, all profits generated are shared between the parties with 50% of net profits remitted to the United Nations. This arrangement shifts greater financial responsibility to the contractor while creating incentives to increase revenue, improve operational efficiency, and reduce reliance on subsidy funding. The total subsidy for catering operations amounted to $1.4 million in 2025. For 2026, approved subsidy funding was reduced to $1.3 million, with $742,000 had already been spent between January and July 2026. In response to rising operating costs and the need to remain within the approved subsidy level, several cost control and revenue enhancement measures were implemented. To help offset increases in food, labor, and other direct operating costs, cafe prices were increased by 5% in May 2026. Cafe operating hours were also reduced to better align staffing levels with customer demand and lower overall labor expenses. In addition, a tiered pricing structure was introduced at the visitor cafe, which primarily serves external visitors. Effective 1st March 2026, retail prices for visitors were increased by 20% to better reflect the higher cost of service delivery and generate additional revenue. On ICT matters, DOS and the Office of Information and Communication Technology are committed to ensure the efficient delivery of ICT services. To this end, we have made targeted investments to modernize critical services. My colleague, Chief of Service and Acting Director of the Operational Support Division, Mrs. Tata Velayo, will share more details. Finally, co-chairs, distinguished delegates and colleagues, I would like to thank you for your continuing engagement and support. I look forward to your questions and comments. Thank you.

I thank the director for the department for operational support. I now give the floor to Miss Christine Tata Vallejo, acting director of operational support of the Office of Information and Communications Technology.

Thank you, distinguished co-chairs, excellencies, members of the ad hoc working group and colleagues. Good day. I'm pleased to speak on ICT matters on behalf of the Assistant Secretary General and Chief Information Technology Officer, Mr. Bernardo Mariano Jr. With your support, ICT matters, ICT remains a core enabler of the General Assembly's vital work. We are strengthening enterprise ICT capabilities, modernizing core infrastructure, and advancing digital accessibility. This commitment is reflected in the services that we provide every day. Our broadcast and conferencing systems support open and closed captioning, real-time transcription, high-quality audio for multilingual interpretation, and accessible displays. We are also systematically advancing accessibility across our websites, applications, and digital services. With regard to the work that OICT does for the General Assembly directly and indirectly as part of our support, the liquidity crisis requires us to prioritize the most urgent technology upgrades and equipment replacements across the UN campus that support member states. The Secretariat had originally proposed a broader five-year project to modernize technologies and all intergovernmental conference rooms, subject to funding availability. However, given the current constraints, we are re-scoping to focus first on the most critical and deteriorating equipment. Our immediate proposal is to upgrade the technologies in the GA Hall and Conference Room 7, and we intend to procure equipment in 2027 and install in 2028. Timings of the work will continue to be coordinated with our Facilities colleagues in DOS for furniture and lighting work, as well as room availability with colleagues in DGACM. Beyond liquidity related issues, we continue to face challenges arising from growing ICT security demands and the need to modernize legacy technologies while maintaining uninterrupted services. Addressing these challenges require continued prioritization and collaboration across the secretariat. And while AI presents opportunities to improve the way we work, Any deployment must remain consistent with UN principles on responsible use of AI and ICT security risks are effectively mitigated. We look forward to continuing our engagement with member states as we continue to implement practical, secure and inclusive digital solutions. Thank you very much.

I thank the Acting Director of Operational Support of the Office of Information and Communications Technology. I now give the floor to Mr. Moses Abelian, Under-Secretary General for the General Assembly and Conference Management.

Co-Chairs, thank you, distinguished delegates, good morning. Thank you for inviting me to brief you on the work of the DGACM. In this brief update, I will focus on three provisions of the GA resolution 79327. In paragraph 28 of resolution 79327, The General Assembly decided to simplify the adoption of draft resolutions and decisions recommended by the main committees in their reports. During the current session, we organized briefings for delegates for each main committee immediately before the plenary meetings at which action was taken on the respective reports. The streamlined process, the so-called one gavel approach, which was one of the outcomes of the resolution 79/327, has reduced the time required for consideration. I'll just give you one example. If you take the first committee reports, it took 268 minutes during the 79th session to approve all those reports. But at the 88th session, using the one gavel approach, with introduction with that approach, it took only 155 minutes. So that's how you were able with that revitalization to come up with reducing time for adoption of the reports in the General Assembly. In paragraph 30 of the resolution 79327, the GA decided to amend its rules of procedures, as you recall, with effect from the opening of the 80th session. Accordingly, we issued the revised rules in six official languages on the first day of that session. In paragraph 36 of the GA resolution, welcome the rollout of the iGov platform, recognizing its contribution to transparency, efficiency of the work of Assembly and its subsidiary bodies. It also requested that the platform be extended to include publicly available information on the work of the subsidiary bodies. I would like to report that to date, information on 25 organs has been incorporated already in iGov platform. I have no choice, I have to use the word liquidity also in my remarks. As you know, as I indicated in my briefing last year, we are continuing to be affected by the liquidity constraints. We are fully committed to improve the efficiency of our support to Member States deliberations, decision making. However, the implementation of certain requests has had to be delayed including the request contained in the resolution 77335 to create an e-delegate web form for submission of reasonable accommodation requests. Unfortunately, the department does not currently have the financial or human resources required to develop the form. And against this backdrop, we observed an increasing number of resolutions that call for new activities and mandates to be implemented within existing resources. It is nearly 50 resolutions with such a wording during this current 80th session. And given the financial situation, this approach simply cannot be sustained indefinitely. As reported in the proposed programme budget for 2027, we provide technical secretariat services to the General Assembly, including to co-facilitate appointed by the President of the General Assembly for informal consultation on draft resolutions. The number of these processes has increased significantly over the years. At the same time, resources in 2025, 2026 have meant that the General Assembly Kosovo Affairs Division is no longer able to provide in-person coverage for every meeting. I think currently we have 16, 17 co-facilitator processes. Nonetheless, we continued to provide procedural advice and organizational support, continued for all informal consultations, enabling those processes proceed effectively. And beyond intergovernmental services, the current funding environment has required the JSCM to contain our own expenditures. We prioritize meetings included in the official calendar. We enforce scheduled meeting hours more rigorously. accelerate the processing of documentation and reduce reliance on external capacity and outsourcing. These measures are intended to preserve core services within the resources available. In addition of implementing provisions of resolution 79327, we continue to support improvement initiatives across the intergovernmental bodies. In particular, by our own initiative, we advised rapporteurs on ways to streamline main committee reports, contributing to substantial reduction in their length. And just to give an example, third committee, one of the biggest number of the reports, until 79 session had 18 reports in 567 pages. At the 80th session, it was reduced to one document in 92 pages. So that's how significantly it has changed. Co-Chairs, in closing, I wish to reaffirm our commitment to supporting your work, that of the General Assembly, ECOSOC and other intergovernmental bodies, and I look forward for your comments and observations. Thank you.
I thank the Under-Secretary-General for General Assembly and Conference Management. I now give the floor to my fellow co-chair, Ambassador Furuta.

Thank you, Ambassador Williams. I have to say that after the UNGA's Belgrade statement is the first time that I think we quantify the impact of some of the provisions in the resolution, and I think that's very much welcome. Colleagues, we open now the floor for comments, questions from delegations. I would encourage you to press your microphone button. If you speak on behalf of a group, just approach the speakers list table to the left and to my left, to your right. We have several requests for the floor. I have Australia on behalf of CANS, Algeria on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, Switzerland on behalf of the ACT Group. We have Portugal and we have several other member states. We'll take them one by one. Australia on behalf of Cairns, please you have the floor to be followed by Algeria. Did you press the microphone? You do, right? Australia?
I can speak loudly.
Yes, I know you can.

Okay, here we are, that works. Well, thank you co-chairs and can I thank each of the briefers on what I think was a really useful set of presentations this morning and it gives us a very real sense of how change is being affected, what some of the challenges are and where we as member states can best reflect on how we contribute to next steps. Obviously, the agreement last year to resolution 79327 was an important step. However, we all know that the credibility of our efforts will not be measured by commitments adopted, but the actual implementation. We make three points as CANS. First, we must contain and reduce the General Assembly's growing workload. We've heard this clearly from the briefers this morning, and it's something which we need to own and address amongst ourselves. At a time of significant financial pressure on the United Nations, we simply cannot continue adding mandates, meetings and resolutions without equal attention to impact, efficiencies, prioritization and delivery. Through resolution 79/327 and 80/251, Member States committed to exercising more discipline in the creation of mandates and the avoidance of unnecessary duplication. As Member States, we must implement these commitments without delay. In this regard, from our CANS perspective, one practical measure would be for Member States to implement fully the moratorium on new international days, weeks, months and years. A moratorium on commemorative mandates during the 81st and 82nd sessions was established in response to longstanding concerns about the cumulative burden they were placed on the system. Such reforms will definitely push us towards a General Assembly that spends less time on managing processes and more time on delivering outcomes. And we consider this will be critical not only to gain efficiencies but to restore trust and relevance in the institution. We all know that each one of us has our particular favourite mandate and our particular favourite resolutions. So we need to own the fact that collectively we need to come together to divest ourselves of unnecessary additions and unnecessary sort of busyness. Second, General Assembly revitalization must proceed alongside broader reform. CANS welcomes progress already achieved on working method reform of the main committees, including the recent second mini decision on revitalization measures. We encourage all main committees to apply revitalization principles to their own work. And specifically, we encourage all committees to bring forward proposals that expand the use of biennial and triennial reporting cycles, reduce repetition and elimination of duplication, encourage member states to exercise restraint and to limit the creation of new agenda items and to maximize the utilization of digital tools. And as the incoming chair of the third committee, Australia and myself in particular is committed to driving practical reforms that make 3C more focused, efficient and impactful. But any of us who has actually chaired a committee knows how difficult that that is. So, uh, I'll do my best. CANS also encourages closer alignment between General Assembly revitalization and the UNAD reform process. Principles agreed in resolution 80251 regarding mandate review clauses and retirement provisions, as well as ensuring scrutiny on financial implication, duplication, and long-term value of new mandates will be essential if we're serious about building more effective and sustainable United Nations. Finally, CANS welcomes implementation of other General Assembly revitalization reform measures, including efforts to enforce speaking time limits, streamline procedures, and strengthen transparency in the selection of the next Secretary General. We very much encourage the incoming President of the General Assembly to continue advancing a culture of efficiency and accountability. As we all know, colleagues, the General Assembly has never lacked ideas for reform. we've just been particularly bad at putting them into practice. And the 81st session presents an opportunity to shift the dial towards a more focused, disciplined and effective General Assembly. I thank you.

I think Australia speaking on behalf of Cairns now, I think there is a prospect to reduce even more the 92 pages report. of the third committee, right, taking it down. But I think that brings a valid point. Implementation is not only happening in these meetings or in the General Assembly. It happens quite a lot in the committees. And the philosophy of the revitalization resolution adopted last year builds exactly on the important role of the committees on how we member states decide to forego the temptation to put forward every session the same resolutions without any operational change in their nature. So there is quite a lot happening in the committees. And of course, the experience in the committees differs from a committee to another. But I think together we can build on best practices. I now give the floor to Algeria on behalf of the non-aligned movement to be followed by Switzerland. Algeria, please.

Thank you. Thank you, Kosez. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, conveying the movement's view and posing several questions to the representative of the Secretariat during this informal interactive dialogue on the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly. At the outset, the Non-Aligned Movement wishes to express its appreciation to the co-chairs for convening this direct and frank exchange, which provides a valuable opportunity for Member States to engage with the Secretariat on issues relating to the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly. We also extend our appreciation to the senior representative of the Secretariat for their participation in this dialogue and for their informative and insightful presentation. Co-chairs, the Non-Aligned Movement has long been committed to and actively engaged in the strengthening and revitalization of the work of the General Assembly, while attaching great importance to the principle of inclusiveness, multilingualism, equitable geographical representation, transparency, accountability, and good faith cooperation. These principles have constantly guided and must continue to guide the work of the United Nations. Against this backdrop, in the context of today's interactive dialogue, allow me to present the following observations and questions for the consideration of the Secretariat. First, implementation of previous resolution on revitalization. The Non-Aligned Movement wishes to acknowledge the efforts undertaken by the Secretariat to implement previous resolution on the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly and to ensure the smooth and efficient organisation of its meetings and related activities. The non-aligned movement attaches great importance to the full implementation of present and previous resolutions on the revitalisation of the work of the General Assembly. In this regard, we recall paragraph 17 of General Assembly resolution 79/327, which decided that the Working Group on the Strengthening and Revitalisation of the Work of the General Assembly will be convened starting from the 80th session to review the implementation of the present and past resolution. In light of this mandate and mindful of the ongoing financial constraints and staff reduction affecting the organization, could the Secretariat elaborate on the measures that have been undertaken since the adoption of resolution 79/327 to advance the implementation of current and previous revitalization resolutions? Second, multilingualism. The linguistic diversity of the United Nations as a whole and of the Non-Aligned Movement in particular requires the equitable treatment of all official languages, especially with regard to the timely issuance of official UN documentation in the six languages. In this context, the Movement would appreciate hearing more about the concrete measures the Secretary-General has taken to ensure the simultaneous publication and availability of official United Nations documents in all six official languages. Third, proliferation of high-level meetings during the high-level week. The Non-Aligned Movement recalls that, through resolution 79/327, the General Assembly decided that, starting from the 81st session, the number of high-level meetings convened during the high-level week would be limited to a maximum of three, with a view to allowing adequate space and time for delegations to focus on the general debate. We, however, note that five high-level meetings are currently scheduled to take place during High-Level Week in September 2026. In this regard, the Movement will appreciate further clarification and elaboration from the Secretariat on the operational measures or guidelines it intends to put in place to ensure a more current and streamlined scheduling of high-level meetings during High-Level Week in accordance with resolution 79/327. Fourth, Equitable geographical representation. The Non-Aligned Movement remains concerned that inadequate geographical representation continues to persist, particularly at the senior levels of the Secretariat. In this regard, could the Secretariat outline the tangible measures that have been taken to ensure equitable geographical representation and the widest possible geographical distribution of staff across all departments and offices, including in geographical posts at the Director level and above? Fifth, the UN 80 initiative and reforms. The non-aligned movement recognize the importance of ongoing efforts to strengthen the effectiveness and efficiency of the UN. At the same time, we underscore that any reform process, including the UN 80 initiative, must remain firmly ensured in the intergovernmental nature of the organization and be conducted in a transparent, inclusive, and consultative manner with the full participation of all member states. In this regard, The Movement will welcome information on how the Secretariat will ensure that any financial or budgetary measures adopted under this initiative do not adversely affect the implementation of mandates entrusted by Member States, particularly those relating to the work of the General Assembly. Sixth, the Office of the President of the General Assembly. The Non-Aligned Movement stresses the need to enhance and strengthen the role of the Office of the President of the General Assembly, through the allocation of sufficient human and financial resources from the regular budget of the UN. In this regard, the Non-Aligned Movement would welcome information on any financial measures affecting the OPGA that have been undertaken under the UN AT initiative. We would also appreciate clarification of whether there were specific criteria applied to ensure that such measures do not prejudice the provision of sufficient, predictable or sustainable budgetary and logistical support necessary to strengthen the role, mandate, capacity and resources of the OPGA. In conclusion, allow me to reaffirm the non-aligned movement's steadfast commitment to multilateralism and to an effective, inclusive, transparent and accountable United Nations. The movement thanks the senior representative of the Secretariat once again for the availability and engagement. We encourage the continuation of this regular exchange, including through more open, transparent, substantive consultation with Member States in order to ensure the effective implementation of the measures contained in past and present resolution on the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly. Thank you.

I thank Algeria for the statement on behalf of the non-aligned movement. I think we'll revert to colleagues from the secretariat at a later stage and I think we'll address your points as well. I give the floor to Switzerland to be followed by Portugal. Switzerland speaking on behalf of the ACT group.

Distinguished co-chairs, distinguished colleagues of the secretariat, I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency ACT group. Let me begin by expressing our appreciation to you for convening this dialogue and the representatives of the Secretariat for their valuable insights. The Group welcomes the ongoing updates to the inventory chart of General Assembly resolutions on the revitalization of the work of the GA and appreciates this opportunity to engage with the Secretariat on their implementation. In this regard, we would like to hear more about progress on implementation of paragraph 12 of resolution 79/327 with regards to the annual update and wider dissemination of the digital handbook on past practices, data and recommendations for the fulfillment of the functions and powers of the GA. We would also appreciate an update on progress on the implementation of paragraph 36 of the same resolution concerning the extension of the IGOV platform, particularly to the Security Council, to increase the transparency and consolidation of information on its work. In addition to these questions, allow me to focus on several issues that have been put forward by the ACT Group regarding the implementation of clusters one and three of GA resolution 79/327. First, on the selection and appointment of the next Secretary-General. ACTA has consistently advocated for a process that is transparent, inclusive and structured. We very much welcome and appreciate the engagement of the President of the General Assembly in the current process, including the interactive dialogues with each of the candidates, the town hall meeting and efforts to ensure the engagement of the broader global community. We are also grateful for the efforts to ensuring that relevant information remains accessible and up to date on the dedicated webpage as called for by this working group. We believe that these efforts are important for the transparency and legitimacy of the process. The next Secretary-General will be accountable to the entire United Nations membership. It is therefore important that all Member States have a meaningful opportunity to engage with the candidates and to contribute to a process that inspires confidence. We continue to welcome the monthly meetings between the presidents of the GA and the Security Council, particularly to facilitate the ongoing selection and appointment process, and encourage greater transparency around these meetings, This could be useful to shed light on the planning for decision making in the Council and the Assembly, including potential timing and results of straw polling processes. Second, on the role of the General Assembly in maintaining international peace and security, we welcome the commitments contained in the Pact for the Future to strengthen the Security Council's relationship with the GA and to further enhance the Assembly's contribution to the maintenance of international peace and security. The pact explicitly calls for a stronger coordination between the two organs. ACT strongly supports a more effective and mutually reinforcing relationship between the GA and the Security Council in full respect of their respective mandates under the Charter. Resolution 79327 provides an important basis for strengthening this relationship. In this regard, ACT supports efforts towards a more analytical, substantive and responsive annual report from the Council to the Assembly and welcomes the convening of the annual dialogue in January between the Council and the Assembly on the report's content prior to its drafting. Distinguished co-chairs, distinguished colleagues of the Secretariat, we believe that a stronger relationship between the GA and the other main organs of the UN, grounded in the Charter, Transparency and mutual respect will strengthen the UN as a whole. AG stands ready to contribute constructively to these efforts. Thank you.

I think Switzerland speaking on behalf of the AG group. We have the following speakers. We have Portugal, Honduras, Ecuador, Indonesia, Russian Federation, and the list continues. I give the floor to Portugal to be followed by Honduras. Portugal, please.

Thank you, co-chair. We thank the co-chairs for their leadership in the working group and for convening this interactive dialogue. We also thank the representatives of the secretariats for their insightful and very useful presentations today. Portugal aligns itself with the statement delivered by the ACT group. We highly value efforts to implement resolutions on the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly, including 79327. Revitalizing the Assembly means strengthening its credibility and responsiveness. I take this opportunity to raise two specific questions. On multilingualism, Portugal welcomes the recognition in resolution 79327 of multilingualism as a core and fundamental value of the organization. Preserving equal treatment of the six official languages, as well as the use of non-official languages where appropriate, can further broaden the reach of the United Nations and bring its work closer to the peoples it serves. Portugal is proud to support DGC's work and its unit in Portuguese. We know that liquidity is a challenge in this respect. Besides liquidity, how could Member States best support the Secretariat in ensuring that the UN reaches people in other languages, including, for instance, during the High Level Week? Linked to the previous question, but also in a more general context, Portugal welcomes efforts aimed at modernisation, digitalisation and greater efficiency in the provision of support to intergovernmental processes. We know that the Secretariat is already working to improve the usage of artificial intelligence in its daily work. We heard that in some of your presentations. Could you perhaps share best practices being implemented by the Secretariat on AI usage and also how Member States can both support and benefit from these new tools. Thank you.
I think Portugal, I give the floor to Honduras to be followed by Ecuador. Honduras, please.

Excellencies distinguished delegates the operational structure of our general assembly designed within a logic of annual sessions today falls short when faced with the challenges and the staggering global reality and there are transport and communication limits that we had last century that now don't exist due to how interconnected our era is now. And this has allowed our General Assembly to become more than just a dynamic body. It's now a outdated protocol based body. Article 21 of the Charter delegates for our sessions gives us the flexibility to evolve. However, we are limited to a calendar that does not correspond to the multidimensional crisis of our time. The current dynamic requires an active assembly that's able to convene at least three substantive sessions per year that limits us in an agile swift response to international threats. We cannot allow the errors and failures of the past and administrative inertia to stop us from acting. The relevance of this institution depends on our willingness to transform this forum into a true centre for constant development and achieving resolutions. We must respect the sovereign equality of Member States as the United Nations Charter establishes for the election of the President of the General Assembly. Otherwise, this organ will continue along the trajectory that will lead to inefficiency and in each session We have to adopt resolutions and revise them when they don't contain language that is in line with the content of the Charter or that promotes violations of the Charter and lets the people of the world down. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Honduras and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ecuador.

Thank you very much Ambassador Williams, Ambassador Ferruta. Thank you very much for convening this meeting and thank you for the comments made. The truth is that having very attentively listened to the briefings of the different representatives of the Secretariat, the delegation of Ecuador in principle, beyond the answers that will be given to all of the different questions asked, we fully agree with what has been discussed to safeguard the achievements of this organization, rescue the organization. The issues raised here should be considered as a whole and they go in line with what you mentioned, Ambassador Ferruta, quantifying how we can achieve this progress. and look at how to continue to improve. Now, on this occasion, I'll refer exclusively to one of the issues of resolution 79 327, which is the selection of the Secretary General and the appointment of the Secretary General. This is an exercise that is approaching its final steps and just some thoughts on this and looking at what we can improve in the future. Transparency and inclusivity in this exercise is not the exclusive responsibility of the members of the Security Council. It's also a collective responsibility of the 193 member states of the General Assembly. Resolution 79, 327 introduced improvements in this area. And of course, We can always improve and under your leadership, I'm sure that we will be able to make more progress without having to wait another 10 years to deal with this issue. Transparency and access to information must be present from the very beginning of the procedure, particularly when the candidates are presented. The General Assembly can consider new measures to facilitate the selection and appointment of a Secretary General, who of course is the highest level official of the organization, we must reflect on ways that will allow us to take account of the opinions of the states of nationality of the candidates, and this would contribute to safeguarding the integrity of the process, including the opportunity for the presentation of candidates. when the candidates are presented so this doesn't disregard the right of each and every member state individually or with other states to put forward a candidate this is the absolute prerogative that Ecuador fully respects nevertheless we must bear in mind that diplomatic courtesy is a recognized principle in international law, is not a merely protocol related matter. A structured, predictable, transparent and inclusive selection process where all member states have the opportunity to evaluate the candidates does not in any way whatsoever contradict Article 97 of the Charter. Thank you very much.

I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador and note the concerns and recommendations as it relates to the selection of the Secretary-General. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you very much, Madam Co-Chair, Excellency. Indonesia aligns itself with the statement delivered by Algeria on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. Allow us to add the following points in our national capacity. We express our sincere appreciation to the PGA and the co-chairs for convening this meeting. We welcome the initiative to invite representatives from across UN Secretariat. We believe that direct exchange between Member States and departmental leadership provides an invaluable platform to better align Secretariat operations with the evolving needs of the General Assembly. In the context of the ongoing UNAT initiative, this meeting even becomes more essential. Fostering this level of engagement is vital to drawing stronger lines of synergy, strengthening coordination, and ensuring that our joint efforts directly reinforce the General Assembly's mandates. Against this backdrop, our delegation wishes to ask the following questions to the distinguished representatives. First, on the critical role of public outreach. Communicating the tangible value of our work to the global public is essential for preserving trust in multilateralism. How is the DG C adapting its global communication strategy to translate technical General Assembly resolutions into clear, measurable outcomes for the global public? Second, on leveraging data for impact. Demonstrating concrete progress requires systemic follow-up after action is taken. How can Secretariat assist the General Assembly in building robust data-driven frameworks to track and report on the actual implementation of resolutions post-adoption? Third, on system-wide coordination. Maximizing organizational impact requires close alignment across principal organs. What concrete coordination mechanisms are currently being developed by the Secretariat to support the elimination of mandate overlap between the General Assembly, ECOSOC, and the Security Council? To conclude, Indonesia reiterates its firm commitment to working constructively with all to build a revitalized and impact driven General Assembly. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation, followed by El Salvador, then Cuba.

Distinguished co-chair, we welcome the convening of today's meeting of the working group in the format of an interactive dialogue among member states and the secretariat. We believe that such a direct dialogue is useful from the standpoint of developing the efficiency of the work of the secretariat and optimizing the agenda of the GA, especially in the liquidity crisis and the general overloaded nature of the body. In this session, work was undertaken to implement resolution 79/327, which is a result of a compromise achieved during the last session, and a number of initiatives that have been carried out have already cut the expenses. Specifically, as noted in the briefing by the USG on the DGACM, there was a so-called one gavel procedure that's already cut the time spent by the body on adoption of resolutions. We believe that this is a useful practice. Nonetheless, going forward, such innovations should be should be carefully considered. They need to adhere to the rules of procedures, multilingualism, the procedure of sovereign equality of member states as well, who have the prerogative to participate in the work of the General Assembly in full measure. What's more, the process of revitalization should definitely not mean redistribution of authorities to the General Assembly to the detriment of other bodies such as ECOSOC and the Security Council. Just showing you one example, there was a decision made to harshly limit speaking times, which just increased the tension in the working groups. On the whole, a lack of liquidity should not be used as a pretext for unilateral cutting of conference services or canceling meetings of charter-based bodies or establishing one's own priorities. Measures to overcome the liquidity crisis should continue to be considered by member states in the context of established procedure and should be agreed upon intergovernmentally and a key role in resolving the situation of the lack of resources. is the full payment by states of their contributions. Madam co-chair, I have a question and in asking it, I would endorse the comments delivered by the delegate of Algeria speaking on behalf of the NAM. I'd like to ask what is the status of multilingualism in the context of the cuts? Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation and I note your concerns and questions and the last one as well as it relates to multilingualism and I will defer to the secretariat on that one when they're presenting their answers to the delegates okay I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of El Salvador thank you.

Thank you very much, Madam Co-Chair. We thank the Co-Chairs for their work and leadership to convene this meeting pursuant to the mandate established in paragraph 20 of resolution 79327. We wish to also thank the representatives of the Secretariat. We take particular note of the difficulties that have often made it harder to implement the mandates of this resolution. Now, our questions are on conference services and my delegation notes with satisfaction the continuous updating of the iGov platform, which for us is very useful for preparation and following different meetings, consultations, plenary meetings, as well as the recent incorporation of the transcription platform. that is an additional useful resource for us to follow the deliberations and consultations. We also appreciate and note with satisfaction the work done in line with the mandate in paragraph 20 of resolution 77335 on the revitalization of the General Assembly regarding the responsibility of the Secretariat to draw to the attention of states and subsidiary bodies instances of overlap with high-level meetings of the General Assembly before adopting measures on proposals for General Assembly meetings on specific dates. My delegation nevertheless does observe that while the mandate agreed is being fulfilled, there are still difficulties in promoting better organization of the planning calendar for these meetings, including the plenaries and the work of each of the six committees. And this continues to cause an overload for delegations to be able to attend all of them. So we'd like to know from the Secretariat what other effective measures you could adopt for Member States to be able to as efficiently as possible comply with this and avoid duplication of meetings and overlap of meetings. We'd also like to know about, we'd like some more clarification on how you will comply with the mandate of paragraph 24 of the resolution. And this is a query that has also been raised by other delegations. Thank you.
the distinguished representative of El Salvador and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba followed by Sri Lanka then Israel who will be the last speaker.

Thank you very much Madam co-chair we thank you for calling this meeting and we also thank the different members of the Secretariat for their briefings that give us a general overview with precise data on the last session and this session and the implementation of the resolution on revitalization. Distinguished Madam Co-Chair, distinguished members of the Secretariat, we align ourselves with the statement made by the delegation of Algeria on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. Please allow me to begin by expressing our Heartfelt thanks to the Secretariat for the huge efforts that they're making on a daily basis to ensure that the organization can continue to function and to provide support to member states in particularly complex circumstances. We highly appreciate the commitment made by your staff. Now, when it comes to the implementation of resolution 79327, Cuba reiterates its commitment to its full implementation. At the same time, for us, it's fundamental that its provisions be implemented in their context and within the limits expressly established by Member States, avoiding expansive interpretations that could create procedural obstacles or restrictions that were not agreed. In particular, the provisions on speaking time limits for statements, the presentation and consideration of draft resolutions and other measures geared towards improving the working methods of the General Assembly. These should not be interpreted as a restriction of the prerogatives of Member States. For us, it's also fundamental to ensure coherence between the different reform processes of the United Nations, particularly between the revitalization of the General Assembly and the UNAT initiative. We would be very grateful if you could tell us how the Secretariat plans to implement this coherence in practice and avoid unnecessary duplications. For example, if a main committee body revises its working methods within the framework of the endeavours to revitalise the General Assembly, they should not demand an equivalent or additional process within the framework of the UNAT initiative. Furthermore, we must also ensure that the exceptions provided for in paragraph 22 of resolution 79327 and paragraph 25 of resolution 8251 are fully respected. We would be grateful if you could tell us what mechanisms the secretariat plans to adopt to deal with the exclusive mandates for this review and to ensure that these exceptions are applied in a consistent manner. Madam Co-Chair, we recognise that the current financial situation poses significant challenges for the organisation and for the secretariat. We'd be grateful if you could go into further depth on these effects, in particular on documentation, translation, interpretation, organisation of meetings and conference services, something that we already received in advance from the different briefings that we just listened to. For us, it's important that efficiency measures be implemented in a transparent, predictable respectable way, in consultation with Member States, in particular when they could have repercussions on the working methods of the General Assembly or on the ability of delegations to fulfil their responsibilities. Cuba reiterates the fact that we stand ready to work constructively to make progress in the revitalisation process on the basis of inclusion, transparency, efficiency, and full respect for the intergovernmental nature of the organization. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba and I now give the floor to distinguished representative of Sri Lanka.

Distinguished co-chairs, we thank the co-chairs for convening today's interactive dialogue and commend their ongoing leadership in revitalizing the work of the General Assembly. We also thank the senior representatives of the Secretariat for their participation and for providing informative presentations. Sri Lanka aligns with the statement delivered by the non-aligned movement and wishes to add the following observations in its national capacity. We welcome the adoption of resolution 79/327 on 5 September 2025 and the establishment of the working group on the strengthening and revitalization of the work of the General Assembly. We see the consensus on this text as a demonstration of the membership's collective commitment to strengthen the Assembly as the chief deliberative and policy-making organ of the United Nations. Sri Lanka highlights the ongoing challenge of achieving inclusive and equitable geographic representation within the Secretariat. Despite repeated calls for progress, this issue remains unresolved and developing countries often raise it in intergovernmental forums. Equitable geographic representation is essential to ensuring the Secretariat's legitimacy and credibility, as well as its capacity to effectively serve the interests of all members. On the UNAT initiative and reforms, Sri Lanka stresses that all reform processes, including the UNAT initiative, must respect intergovernmental nature of this organization and involve full consultation with all members. Conducting reforms outside intergovernmental processes may undermine their ownership and legitimacy. In conclusion, Sri Lanka fully supports this working group's work and its goal of making the General Assembly stronger, more effective and more efficient. We are ready to work constructively with the Secretariat and other Member States to ensure the revitalization agenda leads to real improvements in the Assembly's daily work, even amid the current financial challenges the organization faces. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Sri Lanka, and I now give the floor to our final speaker, the distinguished representative of Israel.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair, for giving me the floor. We would like to thank the co-chairs for convening this discussion and the opportunity for this important dialogue. We appreciate the Secretariat's continued support to the General Assembly and for their detailed briefings this morning. As we stand at a turning point for the United Nations, with renewed efforts to improve efficiency and new leadership on the horizon, we have an important opportunity to make the organization more efficient, effective, and representative of today's global landscape. Israel sees great value in the important decisions the General Assembly will be called upon to take in the period ahead. Hence, we would like to underline the importance of timely communication with member states on matters requiring action by the General Assembly. Member states should be given sufficient notice and adequate time to consult with capitals, consider proposals, and meaningfully exercise the responsibilities entrusted to the assembly. The assembly should not be placed in a position where limited notice would ever constrain its ability to deliberate fully. Secondly, we underline the importance of ensuring that decisions adopted by the General Assembly are effectively implemented and monitored. While member states set the policy direction through resolutions, its success and implementation also depends on the strong coordination between member states and the organization. The scheduling of high level meetings during high level week provides one such example. In resolution 79/327, member states decided that beginning with the 81st session, General Assembly mandated high level meetings convened during the high level week should be limited to a maximum of three. Yet more than three high level meetings were subsequently mandated for the upcoming session. We would therefore be interested to hear how coordination might be further strengthened in such cases, particularly where multiple mandates or processes may intersect. UNAD provided a unique opportunity to foster a culture of efficiency across the organization. Ultimately, any improvement to the organization improves the General Assembly. Efficiency cannot be understood in terms of structures, staffing levels, or budget reductions. It should also be reflected in the way that we work, through greater discipline in the creation of meetings and mandates, avoiding duplication, better use of existing resources, and regularly reassessing whether established practices continue to serve their intended purposes. UNAD and revitalization cannot be a one time exercise. We have only reviewed a select number of mandates, while much broader work remains to ensure that the organization as a whole is coherent, efficient and fit for purpose. If we are serious about meaningful reform, this effort must continue systematically beyond the current session with the same commitment applied across all areas of the organization's work. Finally, revitalizing the United Nations means revitalizing for current times. We appreciated the update this morning and encourage the organization to continue embracing digital innovation, including the responsible use of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. We would like to highlight the positive example the UN transcripts platform sets. We encourage continued investment in tools of this kind that can make the work of both UN personnel and member states more accessible, transparent, and efficient. Israel remains committed to working together to find practical ways to strengthen the General Assembly and ensure that the United Nations is equipped to meet the needs of today. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Israel and I thank all distinguished representatives for their interventions based on the concerns or questions fielded during this session I will now give the floor to Miss Catherine Pollard under secretary general for management strategy policy and compliance followed by Mr. Ian Phillips, Director of News and Media of the Department of Global Communications, and Mr. Moses Ablain, Under-Secretary General for General Assembly and Conference Management.

Thank you, Madam Co-Chair, and thank you to all the delegations for their comments. There were comments from several delegations regarding equitable geographic distribution and geographic representation in the staff of the Secretariat as a whole. Improving geographic representation of all Member States continues to be a high priority of the Secretary-General in human resources management, and that is reflected in the progress that I had shared with you earlier. There are several steps undertaken within every department, including we do have in the compacts of every undersecretary general the targets for filling new positions for 50% should be from candidates from underrepresented member states. The Secretariat through the Office of Human Resources together with the departments also conducts outreach with Member States, particularly targeting those that are on and underrepresented. And with some Member States, we also have specific projects and partnerships so that we will be able to access talent within that Member State to apply for positions in the Secretariat. Unfortunately, as I also mentioned in 2026, this has been a very difficult year in terms of the financial situation, as Member States all know, and we have had to... limit filling of vacancies to only the most critical vacancies and we have generally suspended hiring and improvements in geographic distribution as in geographical post financed on the regular budget really those changes are impacted largely through external recruitment so since this year we have had to limit external recruitment I would say that our efforts have been we have had a setback in our efforts and been able to replace staff who were able who were retired were retiring we will see what the financial situation looks like next year and we hope that there would be some improvement but I just want to reassure member states that the secretariat takes this very very seriously as a core value of the organi of the organization and every department internally does track the progress with geographic distribution on post financed in the regular budget and for non-geographic positions, which are voluntary funding or other assessed resources such as peacekeeping operations to have as wide a geographic representation as possible. I think I will stop there, Madam Chair.
Thank you, USG Pollard. I will now ask Mr. Ian Phillips the director of news and media of the Department of Global Communications for his responses.

Thank you very much and thank you for the questions. I certainly heard that there was a recurrent theme which was multilingualism. This is absolutely core, a core priority for DGC. We did, of course, take a hit in terms of the amount of posts we lost under UN 80, the news and media division, which is the the heartbeat of multilingualism had to abolish almost 25% of the posts. But I want to reiterate that we're finding solutions. We cannot do our job communicating around the world if we're doing it in one language. I'll get back to that topic in a moment. I'd just to the distinguished delegate from Portugal, I want to Again, thank you for Portugal's support of the news and media division. And I want to highlight one particular initiative with funding that is given to us, XP funding. We've been able to create a network of freelancers around the world in the Portuguese, in the Lusophone world, who are able to bring to life some of the topics that are discussed at the General Assembly. And I think that's really important. It can be quite hard to connect with the public with, you know, a complex conversation in a GA debate hall. We are obviously cover that, we stream it, we write about it, but to really connect to people, it's great if we can combine that with real people stories about the theme under discussion. So we're doing that increasingly and the ability to get input from the field, whether written stories or visuals, which we need a lot more of, really enhances what we're trying to talk about today, how to enhance your work. So I really want to thank the Portuguese mission for supporting us because it has enabled us to put create an extra dimension to our work. In terms of AI, we are actively exploring AI solutions and as we all know, every month is getting better and better. But I do want to underline that it still takes significant resources. This is a resource hungry effort. We can't just trust AI to be able to capture everything accurately. So it does require language expertise. It does require human verification. And in DGC and NMD, we are looking at strategic ways to realign our current resources. We have a lot of linguistic expertise, but we also have a lot of pockets of linguistic expertise around different units around the news and media division. My team is looking at ways to maybe consolidate that to leverage our language expertise and to be nimble enough to turn to whatever the challenge is. If we know, for example, where the Russian speakers are, it doesn't matter whether you are a Russian speaker on Web TV or in social media or in UN News. If we know the resources are there, we can leverage that to do whatever job might be required. It is ambitious of us to think that we will go back to the status quo in terms of the number of posts that we have, but if we can streamline our approach to our work, streamline all the many sections and websites that we have, we might have more resources than we realise. That work is under way. I would ask that missions and committees understand what we're trying to do here. We're going to elaborate on it in coming weeks and months about the reforms we want to bring about. Help us push it through because it will help us and it will also help you. Let me think. To the delegate from Portugal about what can be done in High Level Week, I think often the issue with our content is discovery. we're working very hard to create a lot of content, but does the world know it's there? And we have many, many, many websites, and it can be hard to find. So any efforts that missions and countries can make to explain to the media, but also to educational organizations and the general public that this resource is there is really important and will help our work. We are also concurrently looking at ways to consolidate our platforms to have a more user-friendly interface with the public so they don't have to go searching and do Google search and hope that they'll find this content. But anything you can do to underline this resource is there and that it's free would help us. And we are, even though I run the news and media division, we are trying to put more of an emphasis on other audiences too. We try and support the media, but we want to try and support educational organisations, students who are curious about topics in the world. Just looking at High Level Week, there will be very significant discussions about pandemic preparedness and sea level rise, issues like that. We're doing a lot of prep work for that, so we don't just cover the meeting on the day, but we create contextual work could be video explainers, it could be written explainers, it can be timelines of how the UN has got involved in these matters and significant success stories that we've been involved in. All this is educational content that is evergreen. You know, we don't have to think of the news cycle where something appears and then disappears within 12 hours. We're trying to create websites in a more streamlined way where that content will live on. and where, for example, high school students or university students or people, members of the public who are interested can go and find authoritative and interesting and visually strong information on those topics. So help us communicate that that material is all there at everyone's disposal. And I promise it's going to get stronger and stronger in the next year or two. I thank the delegate from Israel for mentioning the issue of transcripts. We've done a lot of work in Web TV to integrate automated transcripts using AI-powered tools. Currently, we have, and this actually will be the first high-level week where we will have transcripts and subtitles available in the six languages. There's a slight delay in five of those. It's just a resource issue.
